1) Determine the patent status
- Search public patent databases (USPTO, EPO Espacenet, Google Patents) for the patent document or published application. Look for filing/publication numbers, claims, and expiration date.
- Check whether the patent is in force. Patents expire (typically 20 years from filing for utility patents in many jurisdictions). Maintenance fees must be paid to keep them in force.
- Example: Use Google Patents (https://patents.google.com). Enter a keyword, inventor name, or patent number and read the claims and legal status field.

2) Analyze the claims vs. your intended design
- Claims define the exclusive rights. Compare each claim element to what you intend to make or use. If your design does not include every element of an asserted claim, it may not infringe that claim.
- Practical approach: Make a side-by-side table listing claim elements and whether your design has an equivalent. If any element is missing, that claim is not literally infringed (but watch doctrine of equivalents).
- Example checklist:
  - Claim element A: present? yes/no
  - Claim element B: present? yes/no
  - If all yes for one claim → potential literal infringement.

3) Consider licensing
- If the patent is in force and your intended use would practice the claims, contact the patent owner to request a license. Licensing can be exclusive, non‑exclusive, royalty-based, or otherwise negotiated.
- Example email template to patent owner:
  - Subject: Licensing inquiry for [Patent Number / Title]
  - Body: Briefly describe your intended use, ask whether they license the technology, and request terms or contact info.

4) Design around the patent
- Modify your design to avoid one or more claim elements. This is a common, lawful strategy.
- Example: If a claim requires a specific combination of components X + Y + Z, explore alternative components or architectures that achieve the same function without using X.
- Document your design decisions and differences to support a non‑infringement position.

5) Use expired patents or open alternatives
- Patented technology in expired patents is free to use. Search by filing date or expiration.
- Look for open-source implementations, standards with FRAND licensing, or technologies offered under permissive licenses.
